_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: This one should be flogged too: that is, granted according to Abaye, who says that [one is flogged] where [the act] is effective: that is why it teaches here that he is not flogged, since what he did is not effective, as he can take her back. But according to Rava, who says it is not effective and the reason he is flogged is that he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One, here too, even though it is not effective, let him be flogged, since he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One.
rashi:a2.1: He may not send her away all his days: which implies that all his days he cannot send her away, so that if he divorced her he takes her back, for all his days he stands under [the command] “arise and take her back.” Therefore he did not transgress the statement of the Merciful One. But elsewhere, even though [the act] is not effective, he is certainly flogged, since he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One.
rashi:a3.1: And according to Abaye: who says that where it is effective he is flogged, but if it is not effective he is not flogged: according to him, why did [the verse] need to write “all his days,” to teach us that he stands under “arise and take her back,” and that for this reason he is not flogged, because it is [a prohibition linked to] “arise and do”? Even if “all his days” were not written, we would know, according to him, that he is not flogged, since [the divorce] is not effective, as he can take her back.
rashi:a3.2: He has violated a prohibition: by divorcing her, but he is not flogged, and the choice is his: if he wishes he takes her back, and if he wishes he does not.
rashi:a3.3: It teaches us: “all his days,” and the verse teaches you that he is obligated to take her back. And now, all his days he stands under “arise and take her back,” and therefore he is not flogged, and not because it is [a prohibition linked to] “arise and do.”
rashi:a3.4: Another version: a refutation of Abaye, who said above that it is effective, since we see here, with “he may not send her away,” that it is not effective, as he can take her back; and that is difficult for Abaye. But for Rava, who said above that it is not effective, it certainly works out, for that is why it teaches here that he can take her back: it is not effective. Abaye could say to you: It is different there, as the verse states “all his days”; that is, in general it is effective, and here, with a rapist who divorced, he takes her back because “all his days” is written: all his days he stands under “arise and take her back.”
rashi:a6.1: And Rava could say to you: that is, according to Rava, who says that no prohibition in the Torah is effective, for what halakha did [the verse] need to write “all his days,” to teach us that he stands under “arise and take her back”? It is obvious, since everywhere too, where it is a prohibition, it is not effective. And Rava answers: if “all his days” were not written, I would say: let him be flogged, because he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One, and then let him take her back, so that he takes her back after he has been flogged.
rashi:a6.2: And the rapist would be [Rashi’s heading; the printed text reads “for it is solely a prohibition”]: that is, this is why it would occur to us that he should be flogged: since the rapist transgresses the prohibition “he may not send her away,” and there is nothing but a bare prohibition. That is why “all his days” is written: all his days he stands under “arise and take her back,” so it is not a bare prohibition, since it has an “arise and do,” and he is not flogged. And according to this version, this is the whole conclusion of the passage.
rashi:a8.1: Its best, yes: that one should separate from the good for the good.
rashi:a8.2: Poor-quality, no: from the poor-quality, for example from the bad for the good, one does not separate; and this is the thing that the Merciful One said not to do. Not that it is an actual prohibition; rather, it is a prohibition that comes by implication from a positive command.
rashi:a8.3: His teruma is teruma: apparently it is effective, which is difficult for Rava, who says it is not effective.
rashi:a10.1: And according to Abaye: who says that anything the Merciful One said not to do is effective, here, with one who separates from the bad for the good, for what halakha did [the verse] need to write “and you shall bear no sin by reason of it,” which implies that it is effective?
rashi:a10.2: The optimal: separating from the good.
rashi:a10.3: He is not called a sinner: since there is merely a prohibition.
rashi:a10.4: It teaches us: “and you shall bear no sin by reason of it,” that he is even called a sinner.
rashi:a11.1: To give the best for this and the best for that: for this is why “best” is written twice, once with wine and once with oil, to teach us that one gives the best for this one, separating by itself from the choicest of this one, that is, from a kind for its own kind, such as oil for oil,
rashi:a11.2: and the best for that one: from wine for wine, and not from one kind for another kind, such as from oil for wine or from wine for oil.
rashi:a11.3: His teruma is not teruma; apparently it is not effective, which is difficult for Abaye, who says it is effective.
rashi:a12.1: It is different there, as the verse states “the first part of them”: that is, the verse repeated it, to make it indispensable, that one may not separate from one kind for another; and therefore, if one did separate, it is not effective.
rashi:a12.2: And Rabbi Ile’a likewise said: that for this reason it is not effective, because “the first part of them” is written: the verse repeated it to make it indispensable.
rashi:a13.1: And according to Rava: who says it is not effective, why did [the verse] need to write “the first part of them,” [to teach] that it is not effective? Rava could say to you: it was necessary to write “the first part of them,” for otherwise I would say that [only where it says] “best… best” may one not separate from this for that.
rashi:a15.1: This is the reading: “But wine and grain, with regard to which one ‘best’ is written”: that is, between wine and grain only one “best” is written, as it is written “and all the best of the wine and of the grain.” I would say that one may separate from this for that: from grain for wine and from wine for grain, and grain for grain, all the kinds of grain from one for another, such as wheat for barley. That is why the Merciful One wrote “the first part of them” again, etc.
rashi:a16.1: Dedications to priests: dedications of Israelites that are given to the priests.
rashi:a16.2: Apparently it is not effective: for if he redeemed them, he has done nothing, as it teaches: they have no redemption.
rashi:a17.1: As it is: that it does not go out to non-sacred status through redemption.
tosafot:a1.1: They raised an objection: a rapist who divorced, if he is an Israelite, he remarries and is not flogged. It now occurs to [the Gemara] that the reason he is not flogged is not that [the prohibition] is rectified [by a positive command], but that the divorce is not effective, since he must take her back. And if you say that since he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One he is flogged, this one too should be flogged, and it is a refutation of Rava; granted, according to Abaye it works out, that this is why he is not flogged: his acts are not effective. And if you ask: since the divorce is not effective, one who has relations with her should be liable as for a married woman even before he takes her back; and with a priest too, why is he flogged and does not take her back? We should say that the bill of divorce does not take effect at all! One can say that divorce is juxtaposed to death, as it says in the first chapter of Kiddushin: death is juxtaposed to divorce, and so too divorce is juxtaposed to death: just as death removes [her] from the husband’s authority, so too divorce, etc. It is ineffective, however, in this respect: this sending away is not for all his days, since he must take her back. And [the Gemara] did not consider at this point that “all his days” is a rectification, because it is a prohibition preceded by a positive command [which is not considered rectified]; that is why it objects to Rava: since it is not effective, let him be flogged.
tosafot:a2.1: Rava could say to you: It is different there, as the verse states “all his days”: all his days he stands under “arise and take her back.” And it is a complete rectification, and this is not a prohibition preceded by a positive command. For that is why “all his days” was needed: that this sending away is not for all his days. This is what the verse means: he may not send her away, and if he sent her away, this sending away shall not be for all his days, since he must take her back. And even though “all his days” could be explained as [living with her] without sending her away, nevertheless, since it is not written “she shall be his wife all his days,” but “all his days” is written after “he may not send her away,” learn from this that it was written to rectify the prohibition. For this is the rule: wherever the verse shows that the positive command refers to [the time] after the prohibition, it is not a prohibition preceded by a positive command. But from “she shall be his wife,” without “all his days,” we would not have inferred a rectification, since “she shall be his wife” speaks of [the time] before any sending away.
tosafot:a9.1: If it is not consecrated, why would one bear a sin? And if you ask: let us say that the bearing of sin is because he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One! Rabbeinu Shimshon of Sens says that this is the meaning: if it is not consecrated, why is “bearing sin” written? Even without it we would know that there is a bearing of sin in it, from what is written, “of all the best thereof,” which implies: its best, yes; poor-quality, no.
tosafot:a12.1: It is different there, as the verse states “the first part of them”: a first part for this and a first part for that. And if you ask: but at the beginning of the last chapter of Bekhorot (54b), Abaye expounds this verse to exclude grain and grain! One can say that the exposition there comes from “first part” [reishit], and this one here from “the first part of them” [reishitam].
tosafot:a13.1: And according to Rava, if the Merciful One had not stated “the first part of them,” etc. And if you ask: but in the last chapter of Bekhorot (there) it says that even without “the first part of them,” [the word] “all” implies [every kind], so you cannot say [it refers to] one grain! One must say that this passage here follows the one who says that “first part” is properly needed for grain and grain.
gershom:a1.1: And according to Abaye: since it is not effective, as we said: if he is an Israelite he remarries and is not flogged, for he is obligated to remarry her, for what reason was “all his days” needed? It was needed, [for] it would enter your mind: if the Merciful One had not stated “all his days,” I would say, etc.
gershom:a2.1: Another version: in any case it teaches: if he is an Israelite he remarries and is not flogged. By the reasoning of Abaye, who said that if one did it, it is effective, let it be effective here, and let him not remarry, and let him be flogged. Abaye could say to you: it is not effective here because the Merciful One said “all his days,” etc.; but in general it is effective.
gershom:a3.1: And Rava: who said that it is not effective, [and] he is flogged because he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One: why was it needed to write “all his days”?
gershom:a4.1: He could say to you: if the Merciful One had not written “all his days,” I would say: let him be flogged and remarry, etc.
gershom:a5.1: Apparently it is not effective, for if he separated, his teruma is not teruma.
gershom:a6.1: And according to Rava, who says it is not effective, what does he do with this “the first part of them”? He could say to you: if the Merciful One had not written “the first part of them,” etc.
gershom:a7.1: As it is stated: “And you shall bear no sin by reason of it, seeing that you have set apart the best thereof.” That is, if you do not set apart its best but rather poor-quality produce, that is a sin. And if it is not consecrated when one separated poor-quality produce, why would one bear a sin?
gershom:a8.1: And Abaye holds that it is effective even without this verse; what does he do with this verse? He could say to you: if “and you shall bear no sin by reason of it” were not written, I would say, etc.
gershom:a9.1: Dedications to priests: when someone dedicates [property] for the priests, they have no redemption at all, even if he transgressed [and redeemed them]. Apparently it is not effective.
gershom:a10.1: It shall be as it is: that it has no redemption.
rashi:b1.1: With regard to a firstborn it is stated “you shall not redeem”: that the owners cannot redeem it and treat it as non-sacred, for example by shearing and labor.
rashi:b1.2: But it is sold: that if it developed a blemish, one may sell it to a priest as a firstborn; for that is why “you shall not redeem” is written, to teach us that sale is permitted.
rashi:b1.3: And it is not sold: as we say in Bekhorot (32a): it is stated here, with animal tithe, “it shall not be redeemed,” and it is stated there, with dedications, “shall not be sold or redeemed”; just as there sale goes with it, so too here sale goes with it, so that it is not sold. And it would occur to us, since animal tithe and firstborn are juxtaposed to one another, as [explained] below, that a firstborn too is not sold, like animal tithe. That is why “is” is written with dedications: to exclude a firstborn, which one may sell.
rashi:b3.1: It is different there: for in that verse it is written “for it shall not be acceptable.” [These words are from the verse on blemished animals (Leviticus 22:20). Sefaria aligns this gloss here; the same gloss appears again at Rava’s answer about blemished animals below (b23).]
rashi:b4.1: This is the reading: “But isn’t there a firstborn, of which it is stated: You shall not redeem; they are holy.” (From here on he explained.) [This heading introduces the next line of the Gemara; Sefaria prints it both here and at b5.]
rashi:b4.2: (This one will leave: that it leaves its sanctity and the substitute enters in its place, because the two of them do not both become consecrated. It teaches us that both of them are consecrated.)
rashi:b4.3: It teaches us: the verse [teaches] that both of them are consecrated.
rashi:b5.1: This is the reading: “But isn’t there a firstborn, of which it is stated: You shall not redeem; they are holy.” (From here on he explained.)
rashi:b5.2: And we learned: in the chapter Elu Kodashim (below, Temurah 21a): What is the difference between firstborn and tithe and all other consecrated animals? All disqualified consecrated animals are slaughtered in the butchers’ market, sold in the market and weighed by the litra, to be sold like non-sacred meat, and we are not concerned about disgrace to consecrated items, because their profit goes to the Temple treasury; as we say in Bekhorot, in the chapter Kol Pesulei HaMukdashin (Bekhorot 31b), that if we permit one who redeems disqualified consecrated animals to sell them in the market, buyers will leap at them and he will redeem them at a high price. But with firstborn and tithe, the profit goes to the owners: the profit of a firstborn to the priest and the profit of tithe to the owners, and for the sake of their gain we do not demean consecrated items.
rashi:b5.3: They have redemption: other consecrated animals that developed a blemish and were redeemed: their redemption money takes on their sanctity and they go out to non-sacred status; and likewise their substitutes that developed a blemish. But a blemished firstborn does not transfer [its sanctity] to its redemption money.
rashi:b6.1: It is different there, as the verse states with a firstborn “they are holy”: they shall be as they are, that it does not leave its sanctity through redemption. And about tithe he does not answer anything now, since [the Gemara] objected only from a firstborn; below it objects from tithe and he answers about tithe.
rashi:b9.1: With any of those brought up: with the blood of one of the other offerings brought up to the altar, which are sacrificed, and the meat is permitted by that sprinkling, since things brought up [on the altar] do not nullify one another. From it we derive [the same] for the other things brought up, and this is what is implied: “they” shall be as they are, even if they were mixed.
rashi:b10.1: Of the blood of the bull and of the blood of the goat: “and put it upon the corners,” etc. He holds that one mixes the bull and the goat of Yom Kippur together when he sprinkles on the corners of the inner altar. It is well known that the bull’s blood is more than the goat’s blood, and even so it is called the blood of the goat and its sprinkling is effective. From here [we learn] that things brought up [on the altar] do not nullify one another.
rashi:b11.1: And Rava: does not derive it from there, for he does not mix them; rather, one gives from this one by itself and from that one by itself. And he holds like Rabbi Yonatan [the printed Rashi reads “Rabbi Yoḥanan”; the Sefaria edition corrects it to “Rabbi Yonatan,” as on the daf], who says in tractate Yoma, in the chapter Hotziu Lo (Yoma 57b): one does not mix the blood of the bull and the goat for the corners of the inner altar; rather, one gives this one by itself and that one by itself.
rashi:b13.1: Avara, avara: with a firstborn it is written: “You shall set apart [veha’avarta] all that opens the womb” (Exodus 13:12), and with tithe it is written: “Whatsoever passes [ya’avor]” (Leviticus 27:32).
rashi:b14.1: What he did is done: and they are consecrated for their value. [These words fit the blemished animals consecrated for the altar (b22), where the same gloss appears again; Sefaria aligns it with this line.]
rashi:b16.1: As Rav Pappa said to Abaye: in tractate Beitza (13b), where we say: first tithe that the Levite took before the priest while [the grain was still] in the stalks, before teruma gedola was separated from the sheaves, so that the Levite caused the priest a loss of two in a hundred in the tithe that he takes, since the priest took nothing from the tithe; even so it is exempt from teruma gedola, as it is stated: “A tithe of the tithe” (Numbers 18:26): a tithe of the tithe I told you, and not teruma gedola and terumat ma’aser from the tithe. And Rav Pappa said to Abaye: If so, even if the Levite preceded the priest in the pile, after it was smoothed, let the Levite be exempt too; why did he specify “in the stalks”?
rashi:b17.1: From all your tithes: the Merciful One says to the Levites: “You shall set apart the Lord’s teruma” (Numbers 18:28), [that is,] teruma gedola. [The Aramaic of the daf, like Rashi, quotes “From all your tithes” (Numbers 18:28); the Davidson English renders the neighboring verse, “From all that is given you” (Numbers 18:29).]
rashi:b18.1: The pile has become grain: and it is fixed [as obligated] in teruma gedola, as it is written: “The first of your grain.”
rashi:b19.1: Any case where there is betrothal: any case where the betrothal takes effect and there is a transgression in that betrothal; and it is explained there that this is a widow with a High Priest.
rashi:b19.2: After the flawed one: that he is a ḥalal. Apparently it is effective, since it teaches “there is betrothal”; for if it were not effective, the betrothal would not take effect.
rashi:b20.1: It is different there, as it is written “he shall not profane”: which implies that he makes ḥalalim and does not make mamzerim; apparently the betrothal takes effect.
rashi:b21.1: And Abaye: if it comes for this, let it say “lo yaḥel”: which would imply that it refers to the offspring alone.
rashi:b21.2: What is “lo yeḥallel”? Learn from it that it comes for another exposition: one for him, the offspring, and one for her: that she herself becomes profaned and becomes a zona, and is forbidden to eat teruma in her father’s house if she is a priest’s daughter. The verse was needed because of her, and not because of what you say, that if one does it, it is effective; for that no verse is needed, since for every matter we say that if one does it, it is effective.
rashi:b22.1: You shall not bring: and we say below (Temurah 6b) that this “you shall not bring” means “you shall not consecrate.”
rashi:b22.2: What he did is done: and they are consecrated for their value.
rashi:b23.1: It is different there: for in that verse it is written “for it shall not be acceptable.”
rashi:b24.1: And fit: even to be sacrificed. It teaches us [that it is not].
tosafot:b1.1: And according to Rava, this “is” serves to exclude a firstborn. And if you ask: according to Abaye, who explains “is” [to mean] “it shall be as it is,” from where does he derive the exclusion of a firstborn? The Ram says that according to the conclusion it works out: for with a firstborn we derive that if one does it, it is not effective, and tithe is derived from firstborn by “avara, avara”; and if so, we can properly derive dedications from tithe by “ge’ula, ge’ula” [redemption, redemption], and the “is” of dedications is not needed to say “it shall be as it is” [so it remains free to exclude the firstborn].
tosafot:b20.1: It is different there, as the verse states “he shall not profane,” etc.: which implies that he makes profanation and does not make mamzerut, and since he does not make mamzerut, betrothal takes effect with her. One must say that this comes from the superfluous second lamed [of yeḥallel]. One cannot say that even without the superfluous second lamed we would expound so: “he makes profanation and does not make mamzerut, and betrothal takes effect”; for mamzerut and the taking effect of betrothal necessarily do not depend on each other, since Rabbi Yehoshua says in the chapter HaḤoletz (Yevamot 49a) that a mamzer comes only from those liable to court-imposed death, but from those liable to karet one is not a mamzer, and according to everyone betrothal does not take effect with those liable to karet. Apparently the two do not depend on each other. But from the superfluous lamed he properly derives that betrothal takes effect with her: if it is not needed for mamzerut, apply it to the taking effect of betrothal. And it is implied that he expounds from the superfluity, since it says: “And according to Abaye, let the verse say lo yaḥel; what is lo yeḥallel?”
gershom:b1.1: And Rava, who said it is never effective, could say to you: this “is” comes to exclude a firstborn.
gershom:b2.1: As it is taught: with regard to a firstborn it is stated “you shall not redeem,” and it is sold; with regard to tithe it is stated “it shall not be redeemed,” and it is not sold, not alive, etc. For he derives from “it shall not be redeemed” of dedications: just as there sale goes with it, as it is written: “[But no devoted item, etc.] shall be sold or redeemed,” so too “it shall not be redeemed” of tithe has sale going with it. But a firstborn is sold.
gershom:b3.1: This one will leave: to non-sacred status, and this one, the substitute, will enter into consecration.
gershom:b4.1: All the consecrated animals: disqualified consecrated animals are sold in the butchers’ market for the gain of the Temple treasury, except for the firstborn and the tithe, whose gain goes to the owners.
gershom:b5.1: And they have redemption: if their blemish preceded their consecration.
gershom:b6.1: Apparently it is not effective, if he transgressed and redeemed the firstborn. It is different there, as it is written “they are holy,” as it is written: “But the firstling of an ox, or the firstling of a sheep, or the firstling of a goat, you shall not redeem; they are holy.”
gershom:b7.1: And Rava, who said it is never effective, could say to you: that “they are holy” comes for this: they are sacrificed, but their substitutes are not sacrificed, as is explained later in this tractate.
gershom:b8.1: That if their blood was mixed with any of the offerings brought up, which are sacrificed on the altar, [it is sacrificed,] since things brought up [on the altar] do not nullify one another.
gershom:b9.1: In accordance with Rabbi Yonatan, who said: one does not mix [the blood] for the corners; rather, [one gives] from this one by itself and from that one by itself.
gershom:b10.1: Abaye could say to you: tithe too is included [in the rule] that it has no redemption, just as firstborn is included [by “you shall not redeem” of the firstborn], for tithe is derived from firstborn by “avara, avara.”
gershom:b11.1: And according to Abaye, who said that if one transgressed it is effective, for what does he need this “from all your tithes you shall set apart”? He needs it for what Rav Pappa said to Abaye: “If so, even if he preceded him in the pile, too.” This refers to what we say: a Levite who went first and took first tithe from the stalks is exempt from teruma gedola, that is, he is exempt from making up to the priest what he lost of his share of teruma gedola. For by right the priest should first take teruma gedola, that is, two in a hundred, and afterward the Levite takes his tithe. But now that the Levite went first and took ten out of a hundred, ninety remain, and when the priest then takes two in a hundred from these, by the amount that is there now, teruma gedola has been reduced, etc.; and the Levite is exempt from making up to him the shortfall from teruma gedola, and gives him only terumat ma’aser, as it is stated: “Then you shall set apart of it a gift for the Lord, a tithe of the tithe”: a tithe of the tithe I told you, and not teruma gedola and terumat ma’aser. But if he went first and took his tithe from the pile, since once it became a pile its processing was complete for teruma and tithe, the Levite is obligated to make up to him what was reduced from teruma gedola. And Rav Pappa said to Abaye: If so, since “a tithe of the tithe I told you, and not teruma gedola and terumat ma’aser,” even if he went first with first tithe in the pile, let him be exempt from teruma gedola. Abaye said to him: But it is written: “From all your tithes you shall set apart”; apparently, even though first tithe is tithed before teruma gedola is taken, “you shall set apart”: he goes back and separates teruma gedola.
gershom:b12.1: And what did you see to include the pile and exclude the stalks? Because the pile has become “grain” and become obligated in teruma gedola.
gershom:b13.1: The offspring follows the flawed one: that is, after the widow or the divorcée, and he becomes a ḥalal. And since it says “after the flawed one,” apparently if one did it, it is effective; for if it were not effective, why does [the offspring] follow the flawed one? Another version: since betrothal takes effect with her, apparently it is effective.
gershom:b14.1: And Abaye, who said it is effective, said that “he shall not profane” [lo yeḥallel] was needed for this: it makes two profanations, one for his seed, who is unfit for the priesthood, and one for the widow, who is unfit for a common priest.
gershom:b15.1: This “you shall not bring” means “you shall not consecrate,” as he says later in this passage.
gershom:b16.1: But if one consecrates them, they are consecrated: for their value, for the altar.
